# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

# Review of the 24-month follow-up of the Varden trial and Halden subset

This report answers most of the open questions from the earlier papers, and it does so with the right tools: a randomised comparison, two years of follow-up, system-log hours and a mediation test registered before the outcomes were known. Its corrections of the Varga and Holm re-analysis and of the meta-analysis are well founded. Its own weaknesses are mostly in presentation:

- The summary overstates the decline in the gain and the strength of the mediation result.
- A contamination problem in the control group is not followed through.
- The control-group meeting figures do not reconcile with the account of the two offices that held a meeting audit.

## Arithmetic check

These figures are correct:

| Figure | Calculation |
|---|---|
| Per hour, timesheets | 0.966 / 0.88 = **+9.8%** |
| Per hour, system logs | 0.966 / 0.89 = **+8.5%** |
| Halden continuers, hours | 34.9 / 40.3 = −13.4% |
| Halden continuers, per hour | 0.968 / 0.866 = **+11.8%** |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 = 100 |
| Staffing to restore counter service | 1 / 0.886 ≈ 1.13 more staff, in line with the stated 12% |

**Cost per contact.** If labour costs rise 12% and output is restored, labour cost per contact rises 12%. The stated 9% therefore implies labour is about three-quarters of total cost per contact. That is plausible, but the assumption should be stated.

**The control meeting figures do not reconcile.** Two of the seven control offices cut meetings by 2.1 hours a week. On their own, they would pull the control average down by about 0.6 hours. The reported control average fell by only 0.2 hours (7.2 to 7.0). For both to be true, the other five control offices must have *increased* their meeting time by about 0.5 hours each, or the averages must be weighted by staff numbers. The report should say which.

## What the report settles

- **The per-hour gain is not entirely an artifact.** It is +8.5% (3.4 to 13.8) at 24 months. This uses record-based output, log-measured hours and a randomised comparison, which are the standards Varga and Holm themselves set.
- **The meta-analysis's "no decay" claim is undercut.** The authors checked the meta-analysis's supplementary table. All four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours. This confirms the concern raised about that duration analysis.
- **Timesheets were not hiding much extra work.** System logs show hours falling by 11% against 12% on timesheets. That one-point gap matters less than many feared.
- **The meeting gap at month six was real.** The baseline figures (7.4 treated, 7.2 control) show the two groups started level. That answers the earlier objection that the month-six gap had no baseline.
- **Fatigue explains less than the Halden authors claimed.** It accounts for only 18% of the gain. That undercuts the original Halden paper's view that reduced fatigue was "the most plausible single explanation".
- **Coverage-bound work.** The county ended the counter arm at month 12 because of waiting times. This is real-world confirmation of the earlier findings.

## Concerns

**1. The summary mixes measures and overstates the decline.** "Fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months" compares a timesheet figure with a log figure. The like-for-like comparison, given in the body, is **12.5% → 9.8%**. That is a 22% decline, which the text rounds to "about a quarter". The confidence intervals also overlap heavily (6.9–18.4 and 4.6–15.2), and the report does not test whether the decline is statistically significant. "Consistent with some fading" is fair. The summary's framing is not, especially from authors who criticise others for comparing unlike measures.

**2. The control group was contaminated from month 15, and the effect is not analysed.** The two control offices that held a meeting audit improved output per hour by 4.1%. That improvement narrows the treated-versus-control gap. Two consequences follow:

- **The 24-month estimate is biased toward zero.** As a rough guide, if offices are of similar size, two in seven offices improving by about 4% would raise the control average by about 1%. The exact figure depends on how much of the 24-month measurement window falls after month 15.
- **Part of the apparent "decay" may be the control group improving**, not the treated offices fading.

The authors should report the estimate with and without these two offices. This could change the interpretation of the decline noticeably.

**3. The mediation result needs a clearer definition of the hours measure.** The logs record "time staff are working on cases". If that means time on case work only, then the denominator excludes meetings. That affects what the mediation result means:

- **If the denominator is case-work time only**, fewer meetings could not raise output per hour simply by freeing time. The 47% would then have to work through another route, such as less fragmented working time. That is plausible but should be stated.
- **If the logs capture total working time**, the description is wrong.

There is also a quantitative tension. Treated offices cut meetings by about 3.3 hours a week more than controls. If case-work time alone still fell by 11%, then total hours must have fallen by more than the 12% on timesheets, unless other non-case work grew. The authors should define exactly what the log measure counts and show how hours divide between cases, meetings and other work.

**4. "Confirms" overstates what the mediation test shows.**

- **The mediator was not randomised.** Offices that cut more meetings may be better managed in other ways too. The authors acknowledge confounding in the limitations, but the summary says "confirms". The control offices that held a meeting audit show that motivated managers do cut meetings on their own, which is exactly the self-selection concern.
- **The test is not independent of the original finding.** It is registered, but it was run on the same seven treated offices that produced the exploratory correlation. More office-months adds observations, but the 14 clusters are still the units that matter. Replication in a different sample is still needed. This partly vindicates the authors against the "post hoc" charge, but does not fully answer it.
- **Small-cluster inference is still not addressed.** The intervals on Table 1 and Table 2 may be too narrow with 14 clusters. Mediation intervals are especially sensitive to this.

**5. The meeting-audit offices hint at something important, but not reliably.** On a per-hour-of-meetings basis, the two control offices gained more from cutting meetings than the treated offices did:

| | Meeting time cut | Per-hour gain | Gain per meeting hour cut |
|---|---|---|---|
| Control audit offices | 2.1 h | 4.1% | ≈ 2.0% |
| Treated offices (meetings pathway) | ≈ 3.3 h | ≈ 4.0 points (47% of 8.5%) | ≈ 1.2% |

This comparison rests on two self-selected offices with a before-and-after design, so regression to the mean is possible. The authors' caution is right. Their suggestion of an arm that reorganises without reducing hours is the most useful design idea in the whole series of papers.

**6. The Halden follow-up has non-response and reversion-timing problems.**

- **Non-response.** Only 14 of the 23 organisations responded. If the 9 non-responders include organisations that reverted or struggled, the 11 continuers look better than the full group. The "survivors twice over" caveat should be "survivors three times over".
- **Timing of reversions.** The original paper reported five reversions at month six, in retail, hospitality and healthcare administration. The marketing agency must have reverted later. The report should say when each of the three reverted, because a reversion after month six is direct evidence about durability.
- **"Upper bound" is too strong.** Without a comparison group, general economic conditions could have moved output either way. "Likely favourable estimate" is safer.

**7. Earlier requests are still unanswered.**

- **Backlog and deadline breaches.** Output per FTE is now −3.4%, slightly worse than at nine months. A persistent shortfall in queued work accumulates over two years, so this matters more at 24 months than it did at nine.
- **Cost per case closed.** This still includes overtime and has not been reported.
- **Halden attrition.** The original working paper misdescribed its withdrawals. With a Halden author on this report, this would be a natural place to correct the record.

**8. Being observed may still matter.** At 24 months, newness is a weak explanation. Staff knew they were in an evaluated trial throughout, though, so an evaluation effect cannot be fully excluded. The modest decline is consistent with a small part of the early gain being of this kind.

## Where the five documents leave things

| Question | Current best answer |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain in discretionary work | About 8–10%, persisting at 24 months in one randomised trial (and possibly slightly understated because of control contamination) |
| Output per worker, discretionary | Slightly below baseline (≈ −2 to −4%), not clearly different from zero |
| Coverage-bound work | Output and service fall; restoring service needs about 12% more staff; in the Varden trial the county ended it |
| Mechanism | Fewer meetings probably matters more than reduced fatigue. The evidence is suggestive, not causal |
| Can the gain be had without cutting hours? | Unknown. This is now the most important open question |
| Original headline (+23.4%, "sector-general") | Roughly double the credible figure, and wrong about sector |

## Bottom line

This is a strong follow-up and the most credible document in the series. The authors should:

1. Fix the summary's comparison of unlike measures.
2. Re-estimate the 24-month results with and without the two contaminated control offices.
3. Reconcile the control meeting figures.
4. Define the system-log hours measure.
5. Soften "confirms" for the mediation result.
6. Report backlog, cost per case, small-cluster inference, and when each Halden organisation reverted.
